hypothesis: starting file

Training on detector boxes (labelled by IoU≥0.5 overlap with ground truth, plus a 5th "background" class for false alarms) instead of perfect crops will improve mAP because the classifier becomes robust to the detector's box misplacement and the background class naturally suppresses false-alarm scores, improving the true-vs-false ranking that mAP@0.5 rewards.

Adding detector boxes that match ground truth (IoU ≥ 0.5) to the training set alongside perfect crops will improve mAP because the classifier becomes robust to the detector's box misplacement while retaining clean class labels, avoiding the probability dilution from a background class that caused e001's large drop.

Adding low-resolution ground-truth crops to training will improve mAP because the classifier sees more diverse examples at the resolution the detector actually operates on, improving robustness for the weak pore and stain classes without increasing compute cost.

Squaring the class probability in the score (conf × prob²) will improve mAP by better separating true detections (high prob for correct class) from false alarms and cross-class rows (lower prob), improving the ranking that mAP@0.5 depends on, especially for the weak pore and stain classes where the classifier is less confident.

Adding a 5th "background" class (from unmatched detector boxes, capped to 1.5× matched count) while keeping GT crops will let the classifier learn "not a defect"; multiplying the score by (1 − prob_bg) will suppress false alarms that currently get non-zero defect scores, improving the ranking that mAP@0.5 rewards. Unlike e001 (which replaced GT crops with detector boxes), this keeps clean class anchors so the 4 defect classes are not degraded.

Focal loss (γ=2, no class weights) will improve mAP by upweighting hard-to-classify examples—especially pore and stain, the two weakest classes—during training, without the negative effects seen when class-weighted loss was tried.

Mixup augmentation (blending two training samples with a Beta-distributed weight and soft-label cross-entropy) will improve mAP by creating virtual examples that smooth the decision boundary between the confusing pore/stain/deposit classes, improving both classification accuracy and probability calibration for ranking.

Switching from two-crop (tight 1.5× + wide 2.5×) to single wide-crop (2.5×) halves the forward-pass cost per sample, allowing ~2.3× more training epochs (from ~1 to ~2.3) within the same time budget. Since the model is clearly undertrained (loss still dropping fast: 0.45→0.27 in one epoch), the extra training should outweigh the loss of the two-view ensemble and improve mAP.

Test-time augmentation with horizontal flip at inference (averaging predictions from original and H-flipped crops) will improve classification accuracy—especially for pore and stain, the weakest classes—by reducing sensitivity to left-right orientation of asymmetric defect shapes, without any training cost.

Reducing batch size from 64 to 32 (with proportionally scaled LR) doubles the number of optimizer updates within the same wall-clock budget, improving convergence and classification accuracy—especially for the weak pore and stain classes that benefit from more fine-grained gradient steps.

Oversampling pore (AP 0.528) and stain (AP 0.611) by 1.5× via WeightedRandomSampler will improve their classification accuracy by giving the model more exposure to these weak classes during training, addressing the class imbalance without the negative effects of class-weighted loss (which changes the loss gradient, not the data distribution).

Adding vertical flip (and 180° rotation) to the existing horizontal-flip TTA will improve classification accuracy by giving the model four symmetric views of each crop, helping disambiguate pore from stain/deposit where orientation cues matter, at a modest inference cost (4 forward passes instead of 2, still well within the 55 s reserve).

EfficientNet-B2 (6.6M params vs B0's 4M) has greater capacity to learn the fine-grained visual distinctions between pore, stain, and deposit, and even with ~1.3 epochs instead of 2 (due to ~1.5× per-step cost), the improved per-sample representation quality should yield better class separation and higher mAP.

Multiplying the per-class score by the classifier's max probability (max over 4 classes) will improve mAP by boosting confident true detections and suppressing uncertain false alarms, improving the ranking component of mAP@0.5 without changing the classifier or training.

ConvNeXt-Nano (5M params, sequential depthwise conv + LayerNorm blocks) captures fine-grained texture differences between pore/stain/deposit better than EfficientNet-B0's compound-scaling architecture at similar compute cost, improving the weak pore (0.528) and stain (0.611) APs.

Increasing IMG_SIZE from 160 to 224 aligns the input resolution with the pretrained EfficientNet-B0 weights (trained at 224×224) and gives ~40% more pixel detail for small defects like pores (the weakest class at AP 0.528), improving classification accuracy despite the ~2× per-step cost reducing training from ~2 to ~1 epoch.

With only ~660 training steps (≈2.5 epochs), the model is undertrained and the cosine schedule decays the LR to near-zero before meaningful convergence on weak classes (pore 0.537, stain 0.612). Doubling the peak LR from 1e-3 to 2e-3 should accelerate feature adaptation in the limited steps available, with AdamW's adaptive scaling keeping training stable at this step count.

Reducing IMG_SIZE from 224 to 192 cuts per-step cost by ~26% (fewer pixels in both data pipeline and model), yielding ~35% more training steps (≈880 vs 660). Since the model is clearly undertrained (loss still dropping 0.52→0.29 after only 2 epochs), the extra updates should improve classification—especially for pore (AP 0.537) and stain (AP 0.612)—more than the 14% linear resolution loss hurts.

Replacing the score `conf × prob[c]` with `conf × (prob[c] − max_other_prob)` (the class margin) will improve mAP because it directly measures how much the model prefers the predicted class over alternatives: true detections with a clear winner get a large margin, while false alarms (where the model is uncertain and probabilities are spread) get near-zero margins, improving the ranking between true and false detections that mAP@0.5 rewards.

The cosine LR schedule decays to near-zero in the last ~20% of training (~125 of 660 steps), wasting that time at negligible LR while the loss is still dropping fast (0.52→0.29). Raising the minimum LR multiplier from 1e-3 to 0.1 keeps the model learning at 10% peak LR during that phase, effectively adding ~100 meaningful training steps and improving convergence for the weak pore and stain classes.

tf_efficientnetv2_b0 has a more modern architecture (squeeze-and-excitation blocks, improved scaling strategy) than efficientnet_b0, which should produce better discriminative features for the fine-grained pore/stain/deposit distinctions. Even though it is ~1.5× slower per step (reducing ~660 steps to ~440), the per-step quality gain from the superior architecture should more than compensate for the reduced training duration.

MobileNetV3-Large has ~44% fewer FLOPs than EfficientNet-B0 at 224×224, enabling ~45% more training steps (≈950 vs 660) within the same wall-clock budget. The extra training epochs (≈3.6 vs 2.5) should improve convergence on the weak pore and stain classes, raising mAP.

Label smoothing (0.1) will improve mAP by preventing the model from becoming overconfident on training examples, yielding better-calibrated class probabilities that improve the ranking component of mAP—true defects get higher scores relative to false alarms, which the model has never seen during training.

The classifier only ever sees detector boxes at inference, so upweighting the matched detector boxes (IoU≥0.5) 2× relative to GT crops during training will reduce the train/inference distribution gap and improve mAP, especially for the weak pore and stain classes where box misplacement is most damaging.

Replacing AdamW (LR=1e-3, wd=0.05) with SGD+momentum (LR=0.1, momentum=0.9, wd=1e-4) will improve mAP because SGD with momentum is the standard and often superior optimizer for fine-tuning pretrained CNNs: larger effective steps with momentum help escape flat regions of the loss landscape that Adam's adaptive per-parameter scaling can get stuck in, and the lower L2 regularization (1e-4 vs 0.05 decoupled) avoids over-regularizing a model that is already undertrained (loss still dropping 0.52→0.29 after 2.5 epochs).

runs.error:
Score 0.4765 is far below the current best (0.6411). Such a drop almost always means a bug (wrong class order, wrong box format, broken normalisation, a model that did not train), not a bad idea. Log tail:
train 26347 boxes (14128 gt + 12219 det), eval 41879 detections, 2255 images (17s)
epoch 0: loss 1.5227, 411 steps, 95s
epoch 1: loss 0.7230, 652 steps, 125s
done: 2 epochs, 652 steps, 71814 prediction rows, 165s total

hypothesis: The raw YOLOv7-tiny confidence is likely miscalibrated (overconfident on false alarms), so replacing it with a histogram-calibrated "P(defect | conf)" estimated from the ~12k training detector boxes should improve the ranking component of mAP—true defects get a more accurate boost while false alarms are suppressed more effectively.

The weak classes (pore 0.537, stain 0.612) are small/textural defects, so input detail is likely the bottleneck: the 160→224 jump (e016) was the biggest recent gain. Classifying eval crops at 256×256 while training stays at 224 gives ~30% more pixels of the same region at test time without losing any of the 660 training steps, and should lift pore/stain AP if resolution is limiting.

The detector's boxes are misaligned with ground truth by up to ~20-30% of the box size (IoU 0.5-0.7 range), but the current training jitter (±10% center, 0.85-1.2× side) underestimates this misplacement. Doubling the jitter to ±20% center and 0.7-1.4× side better matches the detector's actual error distribution, improving robustness especially for small defects (pore, AP 0.537) where relative box misplacement most changes the visible content.

The undertrained model (2 epochs, loss still dropping 0.52→0.29) produces overly uniform softmax probabilities, compressing the score gap between true and false detections. Dividing logits by T=0.7 before softmax sharpens the class distribution, improving the ranking quality that mAP@0.5 depends on.

Removing the H-flip TTA (which gave no measurable gain, e009: 0.6386→0.6387) and reducing the prediction reserve from 55s to 40s frees ~15s for additional training steps (~14% more, 660→~750), improving convergence of the clearly undertrained model (loss still dropping 0.52→0.29) and boosting mAP, especially for the weak pore and stain classes.

Curriculum training—first learning on clean GT crops (60% of budget) to establish class boundaries, then fine-tuning on detector boxes (40%) to adapt to the inference distribution—will improve mAP because the model won't be confused by noisier detector boxes during initial learning, yielding better representations for the weak pore and stain classes.

RegNetY-016 (0.9M params) is ~3x faster per forward/backward step than EfficientNet-B0 (4M params), enabling ~2000 training steps (vs 660) within the same wall-clock budget. The 3x more optimizer updates should significantly improve convergence—especially for the weak pore (0.537) and stain (0.612) classes—while the SE attention blocks in RegNet provide sufficient discriminative capacity for 4-class defect classification.

hypothesis: Training at 160×160 (≈2× fewer pixels per step) while keeping inference at 224×224 will roughly double training steps (≈1300 vs 660), improving convergence for the weak pore/stain classes, while the higher-res inference preserves the detail that gave the 224 gain in e016.

mAP@0.5 decomposes into independent per-class rankings, but the softmax couples all four class scores (they must sum to 1), distorting each class's ranking. Replacing CE with 4 independent BCE sigmoid heads lets each class score be optimized directly as P(class|box), which should improve the ranking of true detections vs false alarms per class.

The cosine schedule decays LR to near-zero over ~630 of 660 steps, but the model is clearly undertrained (loss still dropping 0.52→0.29). Replacing cosine decay with constant LR after the 5% warmup keeps the full learning rate active throughout, giving the weak pore/stain classes more effective training updates.

Random erasing (Cutout-style) during training will improve mAP by forcing the model to rely on multiple spatial regions rather than a single texture patch, improving robustness to the detector's box misplacement and helping the weak pore/stain classes which are small and textural.

Reducing the crop context from 2.5× to 2.0× gives the model a tighter view of the defect, reducing the diluting effect of surrounding weld bead and improving discrimination between pore (small circular holes) and stain (larger irregular patches) — the two weakest classes at AP 0.537 and 0.612.

The weld images almost certainly have a very different intensity distribution from ImageNet (likely narrow dynamic range, near-grayscale), so the hardcoded ImageNet mean/std suboptimally scales inputs to the pretrained stem. Computing normalization constants from the actual training images will produce better-conditioned features, improving classification—especially for the weak pore and stain classes.

Adding an auxiliary 2-group CE loss ({pore, stain} vs {deposit, discontinuity}) provides an additional learning signal that separates "small/dark" defects from "structural" defects, helping the weak pore (0.537) and stain (0.612) classes without changing the architecture or data.
